h1: Selling beer across state borders in India and the permits involved
title: Selling Beer Across Indian State Borders | Craft Beer School
desc: Why moving beer from one Indian state to another needs permits at both ends, what the process usually involves and what to check before you promise a buyer.
teaser: A bar two states away wants your beer. Before you say yes, here is why it is a two-government job.
standfirst: Alcohol in India is regulated state by state, so beer that crosses a border passes through two excise systems. Here is the shape of the process and the questions to ask before you plan an out-of-state launch.
sections:
Under the Constitution, alcohol is a state subject. Each state writes its own excise rules, sets its own duties and runs its own licensing. That is why craft beer rules differ so much from state to state.

When beer moves from the state where it is brewed to a state where it will be sold, both governments want a say. The state of origin needs to know the beer left legally and that its own duties are handled or exempted. The receiving state wants its own duty paid and its own record of every case that comes in. Nothing about this is quick.
First question: can your licence sell outside the premises at all?

Many Indian microbrewery licences are written for a brewpub. They allow you to brew and serve on your own premises and often nothing else. Some states permit limited takeaway sales. Very few let a microbrewery supply other outlets.

If your licence is of that kind, cross-border sales are off the table until you hold a licence that permits manufacture for wider sale. That usually means a brewery licence with bottling or kegging for trade, or brewing under contract at a licensed brewery that already ships across states. Read your licence before you read anything else.

Names and forms differ by state, but an interstate movement of beer typically involves something like this:

  • Brand and label registration in the receiving state. Most states want each brand and label approved before it can be sold there, usually with a fee and a renewal cycle.
  • An import permit from the receiving state, often applied for by the licensed importer or wholesaler there, stating the brand, pack sizes and quantity.
  • An export permit or pass from the state of origin, which lets the consignment leave.
  • A transport permit that travels with the vehicle and names the route, seals and validity period.
  • Duty and fees in the receiving state, paid before or on arrival depending on the system.

Several states now run these steps through online excise portals with track-and-trace labels. Others are still partly on paper. Either way, the rules and fees change, so check the current notification in both states or ask a licensing consultant who works there.
Who you sell to on the other side

In most states you will not sell directly to a bar. Beer enters through a licensed wholesaler, a state corporation or a distributor holding the right licence. That party often handles the import permit and the receiving state's duty. It also takes a margin and sets payment terms. Our guide to beer distribution in India covers how those relationships work.

Price builds up fast. Your ex-brewery price, origin state charges, freight, receiving state duty, the wholesaler margin and the retailer margin all stack before the customer sees a number. Model the shelf price before you sign anything. A beer that is good value at home can land as one of the most expensive bottles in the fridge.
Freight is a quality question too

The paperwork gets the attention, but the truck is where beer gets hurt. A consignment that waits at a state checkpost in summer, in an unrefrigerated container, can sit above 40 °C for hours. Hoppy beer goes stale. Unpasteurised beer can referment. Plan for refrigerated transport or ship only beers that tolerate heat. Time the dispatch so it does not arrive on a holiday when the receiving godown is shut.

Ask the wholesaler how they store stock once it arrives. A warehouse that keeps your cases at ambient temperature for six weeks undoes the care you took in the brewery. Agree a maximum age for beer on the shelf and a plan for stock that passes it. Fresh beer in another state is a logistics promise as much as a brewing one.

Make a short checklist before saying yes to an out-of-state buyer:

  1. Does my licence allow sale outside my premises and out of state?
  2. Who will be the licensed importer in the other state?
  3. How long does brand registration take there? What does it cost this year?
  4. What will the shelf price be after every duty and margin?
  5. Can my packaging survive the trip?

If you cannot answer three of the five, the launch is not ready. That gap between enthusiasm and a workable route to market is where a lot of good breweries lose money.
faqs: Can a brewpub sell its beer to a bar in another state?
Usually not. Most brewpub licences only allow sale on the premises. You would need a licence for wider manufacture and sale, or a contract arrangement with a licensed brewery.
Who pays excise duty on beer sold across states?
The receiving state normally levies its own duty, often collected through the licensed importer or wholesaler. Arrangements in the state of origin vary, so check the current rules in both states.
How long does label registration in another state take?
It varies widely by state and season. Ask the receiving state's excise department or a local licensing consultant. Build that time into your launch plan.
